name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Generation and propagation of axonal nerve impulse

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following physiological events occurring during the generation and conduction of an action potential along an axon in the correct chronological sequence:

(I) Application of a threshold stimulus at a localized site on the polarized axonal membrane

(II) Rapid influx of sodium ions \(\left(\text{Na}^{+}\right)\) into the axoplasm due to increased membrane permeability

(III) Reversal of electrical polarity across the membrane, generating an action potential (depolarization)

(IV) Local current flows from the excited site to the adjacent unexcited site on the inner axonal surface

(V) Outward diffusion of potassium ions \(\left(\text{K}^{+}\\right)\), restoring the resting potential (repolarization)

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Conduction of a nerve impulse is a sequential electrophysiological process involving localized stimulus-gated membrane activation, sodium-driven depolarization, local circuit propagation, and potassium-mediated repolarization.

Step 2: Initial event - stimulus delivery
The sequence begins when a mechanical, electrical, or chemical stimulus of threshold strength is applied to a resting, polarized site on the axonal lemma.

Step 3: Second event - sodium channel activation and influx
Stimulation immediately triggers the opening of voltage-sensitive sodium channels, dramatically increasing sodium permeability and driving a rapid inward surge of sodium ions into the axoplasm down their electrochemical gradient.

Step 4: Third event - polarity reversal and action potential generation
The massive influx of positive charge overcomes internal resting electronegativity, reversing the transmembrane electrical potential so that the outer surface becomes negative and the inner face becomes positive, producing an action potential (depolarization).

Step 5: Fourth event - local circuit current flow
With the excited site internally positive and the downstream adjacent resting site internally negative, local electrical current flows along the inner surface from the excited site toward the adjacent site, depolarizing the adjacent membrane segment ahead.

Step 6: Fifth event - potassium efflux and repolarization
Sodium channel activation ceases within fractions of a millisecond as channels inactivate; opening of potassium channels allows potassium ions to diffuse outward into the extracellular fluid, rapidly restoring the negative resting potential at the excited site.

Step 7: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological progression proceeds from stimulus application, followed by rapid sodium influx, subsequent reversal of polarity, local current flow to the adjacent site, and concluding with outward potassium diffusion that restores the resting potential.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Sequence of events in chemical synaptic transmission

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following sequential stages of impulse transmission across a chemical synapse in the correct chronological order:

(I) Arrival of an action potential at the pre-synaptic axon terminal

(II) Stimulation of synaptic vesicles to translocate toward the pre-synaptic membrane

(III) Fusion of synaptic vesicles with the pre-synaptic membrane and exocytotic release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft

(IV) Diffusion of neurotransmitter molecules across the synaptic cleft and binding to specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane

(V) Opening of post-synaptic ion channels allowing entry of ions that generate a new graded potential

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemical synaptic transmission converts an incoming electrical nerve impulse into a quantized chemical message that traverses the synaptic cleft to generate a subsequent electrical response in the post-synaptic neuron.

Step 2: Initial event - arrival of action potential
The signaling sequence initiates when a conducted action potential arrives at the distal axon terminal of the pre-synaptic neuron, depolarizing the terminal arborization.

Step 3: Second event - vesicle translocation
Terminal depolarization mobilizes neurotransmitter-filled synaptic vesicles, stimulating their directed migration toward the active release zones of the pre-synaptic plasma membrane.

Step 4: Third event - vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release
Synaptic vesicles fuse directly with the pre-synaptic plasma membrane, discharging their chemical neurotransmitters into the extracellular fluid of the synaptic cleft via exocytosis.

Step 5: Fourth event - cleft diffusion and receptor binding
Free neurotransmitter molecules rapidly diffuse across the fluid-filled synaptic cleft and bind specifically to complementary ligand-gated receptor complexes embedded in the post-synaptic membrane.

Step 6: Fifth event - post-synaptic ion channel opening and potential development
Neurotransmitter-receptor binding induces conformational gating of post-synaptic ion channels, permitting specific ionic fluxes that alter the membrane potential, establishing a new excitatory or inhibitory post-synaptic potential.

Step 7: Final Conclusion
The correct physiological sequence proceeds from the arrival of the action potential at the terminal, to vesicle movement toward the membrane, exocytotic neurotransmitter release into the cleft, receptor binding on the post-synaptic membrane, and culminating in ion channel gating that generates a new post-synaptic potential.
